title: The financial cost of leaving an abusive relationship
subtitle: A UK case shows why paying for a new home can leave a survivor paying for the old one too.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Annie was paying for two homes, but she could live in only one. After separating from her partner, she paid rent on a new place while continuing to cover her share of the mortgage on the home she had left. The British charity Surviving Economic Abuse documented her experience in its 2024 report on joint mortgages.

Before the separation, a £20,000 borrowing facility had been presented to Annie as money she might one day use for a deposit. According to the charity, her partner instead pressured her to agree to spend it on a car. By the time she needed a deposit, the borrowing had already served someone else’s plans.

Her experience helps explain why there is no single price for leaving. Rent on a new home is a new expense; a payment on the old home is an obligation that may survive the move. Emergency assistance that covers one can leave the other untouched. Annie’s case illustrates that distinction. It does not establish an average cost for British women, much less for survivors everywhere.
